findings.why: 'Other vitamin C derivatives' is a broad, unnamed group and the 40-50% figure is unsourced (CLM-13); by the same molecular-weight maths common derivatives fall well outside that range (some far lower, several above 50%, sodium ascorbate above 86%), so the comparison isn't accurate or like-for-like. A molecule's vitamin C share is also not evidence the serum delivers more vitamin C to skin, so the table implies a performance edge it doesn't show.
findings.fix: Name the specific derivatives compared and source the figures, or drop the comparison and keep the fact: 'Made with Ethyl Ascorbic Acid, a stabilised vitamin C derivative with 86% pure vitamin C content.'

findings.span: The serum's strength is 10%, as on the pack.
findings.why: In an ad about vitamin C content, it never says whether the 10% is vitamin C or Ethyl Ascorbic Acid, and by the ad's own 86% figure a 10% Ethyl Ascorbic Acid serum holds less than 10% vitamin C. Minimalist's position is that the number on the ad is the number in the bottle, so this one has to be unambiguous.
findings.fix: Say what the 10% is, in the pack's wording, e.g. 'The serum contains Ethyl Ascorbic Acid at 10%, as on the pack.' (confirm against the pack).

findings.why: An internal sourcing note in consumer copy; the clarification around it is useful but reads like a draft note.
findings.fix: Drop '(product page)' and move the clarification to a footnote, e.g. '86% is the vitamin C content of the ingredient, not the serum's strength.'

rule_hit_review.why: The headline names Vitamin C without the 10%, and in an ad full of percentages that makes 86% easy to misread as the serum's strength.
'higher than the 40-50% content in other vitamin C derivatives' is a comparative claim against other ingredient forms (see finding).
Here 'vitamin C' describes the ingredient class (a vitamin C derivative), not the hero active stated without its strength; the 10% appears later in the same text.
The header row compares Ethyl Ascorbic Acid with other derivatives.
'Other vitamin C derivatives' names the generic comparator; the product line 'Vitamin C 10% Face Serum' carries the strength.

tone_read: Calm, technical and ingredient-led: naming the exact derivative, its vitamin C share and its pH is classic Minimalist education, with no hype, emoji or fear. But the primary text is crowded with clarifications and a '(product page)' note, so it reads like an internal brief rather than brand copy.
language_read: The form is named precisely (Ethyl Ascorbic Acid) and '86% pure vitamin C content' matches the page's precise wording. But the headline gives Vitamin C no strength and the ad never says what the 10% refers to, the one number an ad about vitamin C content most needs to get exact.
